projectOutComesReport:
The project focused on developing and applying advanced statistical methods to analyze astronomical data. With the increasing volume and complexity of data collected by modern telescopes, innovative methods are essential to help astronomers make sense of the information. Our research aimed to improve how we detect and understand astronomical objects, such as exoplanets and galaxies, using mathematical models, uncertainty analysis, and image processing techniques.

Intellectual Merit

The intellectual contributions of this project lie in the following key areas:

Solar Flare Characterization: We investigate the statistical characteristics of solar flare occurrences and find that the commonly used Poisson generative model is flawed. We demonstrate empirically that aggregate flare counts are invariably overdispersed compared to a Poisson model. We then show that overdispersion is obtained as a direct consequence of intermittent overlapping of active regions, and provide a theoretical derivation to show why the total counts in generally cannot follow the Poisson model.

Modeling Object Boundaries in Astronomical Images: We developed a new, nonparametric method for modeling the shapes of astronomical objects. This method uses what are called Fourier descriptors to represent object boundaries in a way that is flexible and adaptable to different shapes, such as elliptical galaxies or spiral structures. Importantly, we applied bootstrapping (a statistical technique) to measure the uncertainty in these object boundaries. This means that astronomers can now better assess the precision of their observations.

Goodness-of-fit Assessment in Astronomy: We derived the high-order asymptotics for the C-statistic, which is a widely used statistics in astronomy for goodness-of-fit assessment. The theory results in an algorithm that correct the biases given by replacing the true parameter with the maximum likelihood estimate, a routine commonly adopted by astronomers, even in low-count settings where large sample asymptotics do not hold in the classical way. The proposed approach is highly computationally efficient. Our newly developed approach is publicly available on Github and ready for astronomers to use with minimal inputs and/or tuning.

Astronomical Image Segmentation: We created a new algorithm to automatically detect and count astronomical objects in images. The method works particularly well in images that are "photon-starved," meaning they contain very few visible light signals due to the vast distances of the objects being observed. This algorithm helps astronomers quickly identify objects in space and is faster than previous techniques.

Exoplanet Detection: Our work also contributed to the detection of exoplanets, planets that exist outside our solar system. By applying generalized fiducial inference, a relatively young statistical inference method, we were able to provide uncertainty estimates for key parameters involved in exoplanet detection, such as their radial velocities. These advances help astronomers better understand the likelihood of finding habitable planets in distant solar systems.

Broader Impacts

This project has made other contributions beyond the immediate field of astronomy:

New Tools for the Scientific Community: The algorithms and statistical methods we developed have been released as open-source Python modules, making them accessible to a broad community of scientists. These tools can be used not only in astronomy but also in other fields where image segmentation, goodness-of-fit, and time-series analysis are important.

Training Future Scientists: Two graduate students at UC Davis were heavily involved in the project. Their research led to significant recognition, including prestigious awards from the American Statistical Association for their innovative work in image analysis and time-series modeling. Six graduate students at University of Michigan were involved in the projects, two of them have successfully finished their degrees. All students presented their findings at national conferences, helping to inspire the next generation of statisticians and data scientists. The Astrostat course led by the PI and offered annually at Harvard University has benefited a host of students from both astronomy and statistics. 

Conclusion

Overall, our project has contributed to the advancement of statistical methods in astronomy, helping researchers better analyze complex data and improve our understanding of the universe. Through the development of open-source tools and training of graduate students, we have broadened the impact of this work, extending its usefulness to other fields of science and fostering collaboration between astronomers and statisticians. Our findings have already been published or submitted for publication in leading journals, ensuring that the work will continue to benefit the scientific community for years to come.

abstractText:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this I-Corps project is the reduction of the economic and technical barriers preventing the adoption of current and future advancements in machine learning technologies.  Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have pushed machine learning models to be computationally larger and larger.  Relatively few organizations currently have access to the most sophisticated models due to the necessary computational and memory requirements required to train and deploy such models. This lack of access results in high costs for researchers and businesses attempting to apply AI in applications such as robotics, natural language processing, drug discovery, and computer vision. The technology developed here reduces the size of the models and optimizes hardware so that large-scale models can be used on existing systems.  Improved access to state-of-the-art models will accelerate adoption of AI in the economy and potentially drive more rapid improvements in cutting edge AI-based discoveries.

This I-Corps project develops a combination of several innovations in the field of machine learning acceleration. The innovation is aimed at simultaneous optimization at the hardware and software levels. By targeting both levels simultaneously, the technology enables speeds which are not possible by combining existing technologies individually.  The core technology combines model compression techniques, custom kernels and hardware utilization designs for acceleration, and cloud orchestration algorithms. Prior results have shown capabilities to significantly reduce model sizes and speed inference results.

projectOutComesReport:
The goal of the NSF I-Corps program is to train academics to get out of the building and explore the possible commercialization of basic research projects. As part of the program, we initially explored the market potential of a probabilistic computer, one of our main research projects.

Probabilistic computing is often used as an optimization tool (similar to quantum computing) or an inference engine for Bayesian inference, which is a widely used algorithm in machine learning for problems that require explainability and estimation of the entire distribution, not just a point estimate. We interviewed over 100 companies to learn more about the challenges associated with adoption of new hardware, how big the market is, and the willingness to pay for the innovation. Via customer discovery, we learned that the market size was not large enough to justify the time and cost of building custom hardware dedicated to probabilistic computing. Further, the process of procurement for new hardware was prohibitively long and difficult.

During the customer discovery phase, we also learned that many companies were evaluating transformer-based language models as a useful and robust method of processing large amounts of text data. Transformer-based speech NLP engine was another one of our research projects and we pivoted towards this research and technology via another round of customer discovery.

We interviewed over 100 companies solely focusing on the large language models and found it offered a much more diverse and promising set of applications. It also was growing in popularity with many companies working on internal proof-of-concept development efforts to explore the potential use of the technology in their products. The path to production was also simpler as it did not require new special hardware. The algorithm could be accelerated on GPUs, obviating new hardware design. We could focus on optimizing the software stack. A software-only solution also meant that scalability was significantly better and the technology was readily more accessible.

Research members, Glenn Ko and Yuji Chai, co-founded a company called Stochastic to take the technology from the lab to the market. Stochastic is building an AI platform that helps companies easily employ domain-specific AI agents that augment their employees to work more efficiently and automate mundane tasks saving them hours of time every day. Stochastic has several design partners that they are working with to target real pain points of large enterprises and leverage their data and in-production performance to improve Stochastic’s product.

The I-Corps program provides something that cannot readily be learned from academia or anywhere else. It encourages researchers to think out of the box and focus more on the process and challenges of translation technologies and potential economic impact of commercialization. The lessons learned from the program will not only be helpful in the lab-to-market process but the academic research itself as the researchers will have an expanded view of the potential impact as they think about research directions and what they work on.

abstractText:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this I-Corps project is the development of an additive manufacturing-based robotic lighting technology for use in smart homes and buildings, smart lighting, Internet of Things, and building technologies. Currently,  consumers are required to buy many lights, each placed in a single location, that do one thing. This circumstance drives up the buying, design, installation, and energy costs for lighting devices. The proposed technology is designed to offer consumers the opportunity to replace multiple devices that perform one task with one device that rapidly performs many tasks through the use of a mobile application.  Indoor and outdoor adaptive lighting systems using the proposed technology may support automated systems for lighting control.  The benefits of multi-purpose lighting systems also include safety, energy-savings and advanced ergonomic behavior to end-users. This project may advance current technologies for smart lighting and the development of more efficient, compact and adaptive lighting systems, ultimately saving space and energy, as well as reducing lighting design, manufacturing, installation and operations costs for spaces situated in contemporary urban settings.

This I-Corps project is based on the development of an automated, adaptive optic technology that allows for dynamic redirection and distribution of artificial lighting in interior and exterior spaces. The proposed technology is a 3D printing technology for producing optic filters that exhibit adaptive lighting behavior when integrated with light emitting diode (LED) technology, data sensing, and robotic motion control algorithms. The proposed design combines research in materials science/engineering, robotics, and the Internet of Things (IoT). Integrated lighting devices using the advanced optic behavior have demonstrated the ability to dynamically and efficiently control lighting properties such as direction, ambiance, and movement, functions which are not currently possible using existing smart lighting technologies.

projectOutComesReport:
Currently, commercial applications related to adaptive lighting have not explored the extent to which the technology can significantly benefit the health and well-being of users from a photobiological and beyond-instrumental perspective. Based on this problem, and exploring the possibilities of a robotic lighting technology, an extensive customer discovery strategy and process were developed. During that process, a large pool of potential markets was explored through interviews with stakeholders, influencers from areas including LED manufacturing, Life Sciences-specific Lighting, Consumer Electronics, Architecture, Building Technology and Design. From the interview process, it was found that, despite the advanced technical capabilities of adaptive lighting in occupational and living settings, many current technologies do not cater to human factors relating to lighting comfort or usability. It was found that this is especially -and critically- true in the Medical and Life Sciences segment, where, for example, operating room lighting technologies can negatively affect physicians' body posture and comfort during long procedures. Based on this problem, a rigorous hypothesis testing and value discovery process was deployed in the Medical and Life Sciences segment, where technology-market fit was further confirmed through further interviewing and interaction with physicians. From a societal impact perspective, the project findings suggest new, cross-disciplinary directions that bring the science of light and photobiology into places for working and living. Moreover, the project introduces a new educational and problem-based framework for the development of new technologies related to lighting.

abstractText:
The first animals originated over half a billion years ago, but marine life did not reach modern-like levels of biodiversity and ecological complexity until approximately 450 million years ago during the so-called Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event, or GOBE (go-bee). Although the GOBE represents a critical transition between the appearance of the first animals and the subsequent exploration of dry land, this major event is largely informed by a biased fossil record consisting mainly of shells, bones, and teeth. This project investigates how exceptional fossil deposits – which contain the remains of soft-bodied animals – impact our knowledge of marine biodiversity and ecology during the early stages of the GOBE. New investigations of the Fezouata fossil biota of Morocco will lead to the discovery of dozens of new extinct animal species, produce an unrivalled understanding of the organization of the first modern-like marine communities, and allows for an evaluation of the rise in ecological complexity that defines the biosphere today. This project integrates undergraduate students from groups that are underrepresented in geology and evolutionary biology into an ambitious research, educational and outreach program. In addition, the project will produce a unique augmented reality-enhanced natural history museum exhibition in Greater Boston, as well as authoritative online resources for K-12 students, teachers, and the general public. 

This research investigates how exceptionally preserved non-biomineralizing fossil organisms impact our understanding of animal evolution and ecology during the early stages of the GOBE, which caused the largest and fastest diversification at lower taxonomic levels of marine organisms for the entire Phanerozoic. Cutting-edge imaging techniques, such as X-ray computed tomography, will be used to study the Fezouata fossils to reveal new anatomical features normally obscured by the rock matrix. These techniques will allow for the description and characterization of the full biodiversity of the Tremadocian-Floian Fezouata biota of Morocco.  Conducting stratigraphically controlled sampling and working with specimens in museum collections will allow the PI to reconstruct the paleoecology and community structure of fossil organisms from the Fezouata biota and assess their spatiotemporal variability within this deposit. Finally, the project will test how non-biomineralizing organisms inform patterns of ecological turnover during the Cambrian-Ordovician transition and lead to the early establishment of modern-like marine communities.

abstractText:
Enabled by developments in the additive manufacturing of engineered systems with unprecedented levels of compositional and structural complexity, there have been major advances in architected materials that possess exciting mechanical properties dictated by their engineered structure. Within the realm of dynamics, the idea of using engineered structures to produce novel properties has been historically focused primarily on linear waves. This work seeks to understand the propagation of non-linear waves in mechanical metamaterials with application toward control of mechanical signals in larger-amplitude loading (for example, to provide protection during impact events) and toward reconfigurable soft structures (for example, locomotion of soft robots). This research will promote interdisciplinary research and teaching. Students of all levels will learn concepts and techniques from materials science and engineering, computational and analytic mechanical modeling, advanced manufacturing, and sensing. Moreover, the research team will integrate these efforts with undergraduate research programs, outreach efforts, and educational material development at both institutions to provide research opportunities to underrepresented groups of all ages (K-12, undergraduate, and graduate).

The objective of this work is to understand the fundamental connection between geometry and the propagation of non-linear waves in compliant mechanical metamaterials comprising rotating polygons. Rather than limiting the scope to periodic systems as in previous work, the geometry of the metamaterials will be locally tailored, and inhomogeneities will be harnessed to achieve target dynamic responses such as maximal energy absorption, soliton lensing, and locomotion. The multi-faceted research program will intertwine theoretical, numerical, and experimental activities to generate new insights into the non-linear dynamic behavior of mechanical metamaterials based on rotating units. To achieve this, the research is organized into three thrusts, focusing on (1) the effect of inhomogeneities on the propagation of non-linear waves, (2) reconfigurability of system dynamics via non-linear waves, and (3) optimization of geometry and defects via machine learning to achieve targeted dynamic properties (energy absorption, steering waves, locomotion, etc.).

This project is co-funded by the Dynamics, Control, and Systems Diagnostics (DCSD) and the Mechanics of Materials and Structures (MOMS) programs in the Civil, Mechanical, and Industrial Innovation Division.

projectOutComesReport:
Precise control over the nonlinear behavior of material structures is crucial for a range of dynamic tasks, including energy harvesting from elastic pulses, impact mitigation, and mechanical signal processing. Recent advancements have underscored the significant potential of flexible metamaterials for controlling nonlinear wave propagation. This project explored the fundamental link between geometry and the propagation of nonlinear waves in compliant mechanical metamaterials composed of rotating polygons. Furthermore, we developed a framework to automate the design of flexible metamaterial structures capable of performing specific nonlinear dynamic tasks, with functionality that can be reprogrammed in real-time. This framework shows promise in identifying metamaterials that exhibit complex transient and steady-state dynamic responses to simple actuation inputs. Leveraging these capabilities, our platform could enable transformative applications in robotics, tunable vibration control, large-amplitude impact mitigation, and energy harvesting in highly deformable structures. An important outcome of this project is its promotion of interdisciplinary research. Graduate students and postdoctoral fellows actively engaged in the research process, learning to make broad connections across disciplines within a multidisciplinary framework. Developing metamaterials with tailored nonlinear dynamic behavior demands a mix of imagination, creativity, and rigorous analysis—skills that have been enhanced among students involved in this research. Further, the PI  is dedicated to promoting science and engineering to a wide audience and worked closely with Cambridge Public Schools.

abstractText:
Transportation system designers face complex tradeoffs around the number, design, and service frequency of routes, which impact transportation safety and efficiency. This research project will study how to design the best public transport network in congested large urban areas.  It leverages high-resolution data and several modern economic methods to determine the best network structures and discusses how the best network shape depends on city structure and commuter preferences.  In developing recommendations for the best network design and studying its rollout, this project will also provide valuable insights for efficient bus systems during the COVID-19 pandemic and beyond. More broadly, it will provide insights into the design features of public bus systems in congested large urban areas in the developed world as well as in emerging market mega-cities, to the benefit of millions of daily public transport riders worldwide.  The results of this research project will provide inputs into urban transportation designs that improves urban transportation, decrease communing cost, hence improve worker productivity, leading to faster economic growth.  It will also improve the wellbeing of commuters as well as contribute to slowing the pace of climate change.   

This two-part project develops a model of an optimal urban bus transit system and estimate the model with a large, innovative data collected by the PIs for the project.  The first part develops and estimates a travel demand model of public transport in a large densely populated and congested urban area.  The project will use high-resolution micro data on ridership and commuting, variation induced by large historical route network expansion, and a system-wide randomized experiment that the PIs have conducted, to estimate the degree to which commuters value key parameters such as fast connections, direct connections, and frequent service.   The second part will use numerical optimization techniques to compute the optimal public transport network and to synthesize how the optimal network shape depends on factors such as the commuter preference parameters, city structure, and the policy objective.  The project connects and expands upon classic topics in the transportation economics literature, such as travel demand estimation and increasing returns in public transport, by employing rigorous causal estimation and studying actual empirical variation in an entire citywide network of routes. The quantitative methods and qualitative insights from this study have the potential to inform public transport network design in densely populated urban areas in developed as well as developing countries around the world.  The results of this research project will provide inputs into designs that will improve urban transportation, decrease communing cost, hence improve worker productivity, leading to faster economic growth.

projectOutComesReport:
This project explored the design and optimization of bus networks, specifically studying TransJakarta, a bus rapid transit (BRT) system in Jakarta, Indonesia. We studied how changes and improvements to the bus network impact commuter bus ridership, commuter welfare, and the overall performance of the public transport system.

Designing public transport networks involves trade-offs between coverage, service frequency, and direct service. We use the expansion of the TransJakarta bus system to study these trade-offs, using large datasets including TransJakarta fare transactions (fare card taps), bus GPS, and de-identified smartphone location data. We analyze how new direct connections, changes in bus travel time, and wait time reductions affect bus ridership and aggregate flows. Specifically, we use an event study approach observing the launch of new BRT (separated bus lane) and non-BRT routes as “natural experiments”. We use origin-destination (OD) data to measure direct impacts on travel times, bus headways (frequency), and ridership between pairs of locations. In doing so, we estimate commuter preferences (e.g., how much commuters dislike waiting at bus stops versus time spent on the bus versus transfers) and develop and estimate a transit network demand model. We also develop a flexible framework to characterize optimal networks.

This project yields several key findings. First of all, riders in Jakarta are highly responsive to improvements in bus service, but they value some improvements more than others. Examining travel time, wait time, and transfers as decision factors in whether to take the bus, we find that commuters are 2-3 times more sensitive to time waiting for the bus wait than time spent on the bus time. Their dislike of waiting for the bus is stronger for non-BRT routes than BRT routes, and commuters are generally inattentive to long routes. They do not have a particular dislike for transfers, beyond the extent to which these increase overall travel time and wait time. However, these preferences only reflect commuters in Jakarta. Through simulations, we observe that optimal network design changes substantially if these preferences are hypothetically changed.

Second, this project has concrete implications for network design. The current TransJakarta network is concentrated in the city’s urban core, with relatively few bus routes connecting to the city’s outskirts. In contrast, the optimal network is less dense and extends beyond the center of the city, connecting more locations, especially those just outside the urban core. While commuters value wait time highly, reducing service frequency in the city’s central area is not very costly because the initial frequency is very high, often more than a bus every minute. The optimal network also has fewer bus lines, covering fewer kilometers of roadway. With an optimal network, through the lens of the model, bus ridership would be expected to increase by 62% compared to the current network.

Third, this study provides suggestive evidence that increases in bus ridership, following improvements to TransJakarta’s network, are driven by mode substitution—people shift from other travel modes (like private vehicles) to the improved bus service, rather than increasing the total number of trips taken. We cannot detect any significant increase in overall origin-destination travel in the short run (as detected by smartphone location data), pointing to a substitution effect rather than network expansion stimulating new demand, although these estimates are noisy. Thus, optimizing the TransJakarta network would be expected to decrease commute times for both bus- and non-bus commuters. Although, given the initial low market share of TransJakarta, reductions in congestion due to this mode switching are likely limited, and significant congestion relief would require much larger scale shifts.

The broader impacts of this project have been two-fold. First, it has provided tangible insights and policy recommendations for Jakarta’s bus system. TransJakarta now uses some of the technical tools developed in this project as part of its regular operations and plans to continue collaborating with the research team to implement and test further improvements to the bus network, in line with model recommendations. More broadly, this project has provided insights into the design features of public bus systems that are applicable to emerging market mega-cities worldwide, as well as a general framework for characterizing commuter preferences in different settings and using these preferences to model optimal transport networks.

In terms of intellectual merit, this project builds on classic travel demand and mode choice theory, and makes a contribution by linking micro-level preference heterogeneity with macro-level network design. It provides applied insights for transit agencies and policymakers about the circumstances under which transit investments are likely to maximize welfare or ridership. By connecting empirical evaluation with demand modeling, the research illustrates a replicable approach for other urban and transit contexts.

abstractText:
FlyBase is a bioinformatics resource to capture, organize and present core information on Drosophila (fly) genomics and genetics, both from literature and large-scale data generation projects. FlyBase provides an openly accessible centralized resource for Drosophila genetic and genomic data to enable researchers and educators worldwide both in the Drosophila community and broader biomedical sciences community to further their research. Drosophila is one of the premier model organisms and provides cost-effective help in elucidating the basic tenets of genetic and developmental mechanisms. FlyBase has three main goals. First, it curates literature and reagents relevant to Drosophila research, so that researchers can continue to rely on FlyBase to find the latest innovations in the field. FlyBase prioritizes curation of data sets relevant to gene expression, cellular functions, signaling pathways, and results relevant to human biology, and displays the information in an intuitive, integrated, readily searchable format. Secondly,  it strives to be of value to the broader genetics and population genetics communities, by curating and integrating relevant data sets, and developing tools that enable better access to this wealth of data. Finally, it seeks to develop and integrate tools to expand it's utility. FlyBase has a long history of very successfully serving the scientific community in this capacity. FlyBase works closely with other Model Organism Databases (MODs) to integrate data sets and develop tools to enable cross-species analyses.  NSF funding allows FlyBase to maintain its three main activities.

Activities essential to the operation of FlyBase include: Automated triaging pipeline; Full genetic curation with emphasis on genome feature curation and physical interaction curation; Human disease model curation; Allele-based curation of disease models based on the Disease Ontology; Gene Group curation; Curation of datasets deemed to be of highest general interest to the FlyBase user community; Import of graphical abstracts in FlyBase references; Identification of new lncRNAs, anti-sense lncRNAs and smORFs; Incorporation of available transcription start site data into FlyBase; Addition of new anatomy terms; Review and improvement of phenotypic class ontologies; Development of database modules for gene groups and human disease models; Annotation of all Drosophila cell types and curation of scRNAseq data sets; Update of the genomic sequences of all Drosophila Genetic Reference Panel (DGRP) strains; Expansion of a Pathway page resource. To facilitate integrative analyses and approaches FlyBase continues to expand its utility as a platform by integrating and displaying large-scale studies, transcriptomics and proteomics data sets. In addition, FlyBase improves access and display of tools available within the community, and incorporates the most useful data sets and tools for visualizing complex data sets to enable more researchers to take a more global approach to their genetic research. NSF funding allows for continued coordination with the ongoing operation and maintenance of the existing infrastructure to enable discovery in the biological sciences by supporting the computational database pipeline infrastructure of FlyBase data. FlyBase will maintain and further develop the central database that houses all FlyBase data; manage the incorporation of additional curated or large-scale data into the database; produce weekly internal reports and bi-monthly outputs that are transformed into the updates to the public FlyBase servers; work closely with NCBI to incorporate genome annotation-related data into FlyBase and to submit periodic whole genome annotation updates to GenBank. Collectively, these activities maximize the impact of essential Drosophila research on discovery and translation. Through their role in carrying out these missions, FlyBase will continue to help Drosophila research advance as quickly as possible for the ultimate benefit of various scientific communities via http://flybase.org

projectOutComesReport:
During the lifetime of this award, we continued many literature curation and high throughput curation activities.  Some highlights are:

-        We used a system to flag disease-related papers and integrated these into our curation pipeline.

-        Placed an emphasis on genome feature curation and physical interaction curation, with goals of bringing genome feature curation completely up to date, and keeping pace with new physical interaction curation while also addressing the backlog.

-        Human disease model curation: Extensive curation effort were devoted to human disease models, including creation of free-text summaries and capture of the genes, both fly and human, used in these investigations. There has been an increase in characterization of disease-implicated variants using Drosophila models; while these are highlighted in the human disease model summaries, the growing number has led us to plan for a more integrated view. This information is presented in tabulated formats in the human disease model reports and in gene reports. Variants introduced into fly genes as analogous mutations (as transgenes or at the endogenous locus) are mapped to the genome.

-        We continue allele-based curation of disease models based on the Disease Ontology (DO); this curation is compatible with the approach used by the Alliance. A key aspect of FlyBase DO curation is the capture of genetic interactions that ameliorate or exacerbate a disease-related phenotype.

-        We used available orthology data and expand our representation of orthology calls especially as they relate to the other MODs and human genes.

-        Gene Group curation: We continue to update our links between fly Gene Groups at FlyBase and human Gene Groups at the HGNC. This facilitates comparison between equivalent protein complexes and other functional classes.

-        We curated select datasets deemed to be of highest general interest to the FlyBase user community.

-        We coordinated with the DGRC and DRSC to create FlyBase reports for new cell lines added to the DGRC, many of which come from the DRSC.

-        Signaling Pathways We have continued to expand our Pathway resource, using GO annotation as a basis to compile experimental evidence-weighted lists of genes that encode either core pathway components or pathway regulators.

-        With combined funding from VFB[MOU1] (Virtual Fly Brain) and FlyBase, we continued to add new anatomy terms and enhanced the existing terms by an ongoing review process, with a focus on new neuroanatomy terms and definitions.

-        We continued to review and improve the phenotypic class ontology and, focused on terms for behavioral, learning and memory phenotypes in collaboration with VFB.

-        Development of Chado modules for gene groups and human disease models was  maintained and updated as necessary.

-        We actively worked with the Fly Cell Atlas and single Cell Atlas to annotate all Drosophila cell types and curate scRNAseq data sets. We worked with the Human Cell Atlas to integrate Drosophila and human scRNAseq data sets to enable cross-species comparisons.

-        We continued to establish pipelines to fetch scRNAseq datasets from the EBI’s Single Cell Expression Atlas, annotated them, and loaded the metadata into FlyBase as dataset reports.

-        Continued curation of GAL4 drivers.

-        Continued experimental tool report development.

 

FlyBase improved the utility of the resource for the core community of Drosophila research and to attract additional users through a variety of outreach activities including:

-        Community outreach via commentaries and the FlyBase Newsletter

-        The FlyBase Community Advisory Group (FCAG) responded to surveys, made suggestions, etc.

-        Video tutorials round at the ‘FlyBase TV’ YouTube channel: https://www.youtube.com/c/FlyBaseTV.

-        Twitter: We promoted FlyBase using Twitter: @ FlyBaseDotrOrg https://twitter.com/flybasedotorg?lang=en  and on Bluesky. 

-        FlyBase Help Desk: We maintained a project-wide help desk to provide support to users with data/web interface questions or suggestions.

-        Presentations and Conference attendance at the Annual Drosophila Research Conference, the European Drosophila Research Conference, and the Boston Area Drosophila Meeting

-        Publications: staff contributed to several publications in the reporting period.

-        FlyBase Wiki: We contributed to updates of the FlyBase documentation on the wiki and maintained the online resource pages that contain many hundreds of links to useful external web sites. All external links in the resource pages were checked and updated.

-        We continued development of the Flybase website including:

  • Import DGRC cell line information to reports
  • Handle split GAL4 combination FlyBase objects in website presentations
  • Synchronize Batch Download with current FB data types and report fields
  • Process and integrate new Interactive Fly data
  • Repair, removal or replacement of esyN interaction network graphic
  • Optimized usability in FlyBase based on user feedback and observations
  • Enhanced public programmatic endpoints (APIs) to improve data access for external collaborations (e.g.,Alliance) and advanced users
  • Continued security improvements for cloud and on-premise compute resources
  • Continued extensive ongoing activities to maintain the website to include internal and external group coordination, pipeline management and maintenance, security monitoring and response.

abstractText:
This award provides support to U.S. researchers participating in a project competitively selected by a 55-country initiative on global change research through the Belmont Forum.  The Belmont Forum is a consortium of research funding organizations focused on support for transdisciplinary approaches to global environmental change challenges and opportunities.  It aims to accelerate delivery of the international research most urgently needed to remove critical barriers to sustainability by aligning and mobilizing international resources. Each partner country provides funding for their researchers within a consortium to alleviate the need for funds to cross international borders. This approach facilitates effective leveraging of national resources to support excellent research on topics of global relevance best tackled through a multinational approach, recognizing that global challenges need global solutions.

This project focuses on coral reefs – one of the most valuable ecosystems on the planet that are being lost at an alarming rate.  This loss threatens human lives because coral reefs provide food, income, and shoreline protection. Efforts are underway worldwide to rehabilitate reefs, with mixed success.  This project uses a novel approach to rebuild coral reef ecosystems by building artificial reefs and seeding them with biota from healthy coral reefs.  The project will be carried out in Ranobe Bay in southwest Madagascar which contains 32 kilometers of coastline with 13 villages, increasing populations, and growing rates of malnutrition largely caused by overfishing.  The primary goal is to rebuild healthy coral reef ecosystems and increase fisheries catch in Madagascar to reduce the incidence of malnutrition in the most impoverished country in the world.  All aspects of the project will involve local scientists and fishers. The project will utilize cutting edge tools, including environmental DNA barcoding, fisher supported GPS tracking of fisheries activities, and extensive human health and well-being data collection to comprehensively connect ecosystem health to human health.  This project will provide a comprehensive blueprint for other coral reef restoration projects by thoroughly testing a new technology, creating tools to measure success, providing a guide describing the ecosystem to human health data collection protocols. Overall, this project will greatly enhance the equitable and sustainable use of marine resources and will respond to a threat caused by global change, all with a tool that can be applied anywhere coral reef ecosystems are found.

projectOutComesReport:
Coral reefs are vital ecosystems that are disappearing rapidly due to climate change and local human activities. This loss of biodiversity and habitat complexity results in ecosystems that provide decreasing amounts of seafood for local consumption, endangering food security, incomes, and coastal protection for millions of people. We implemented a new reef restoration approach in Southwestern Madagascar to enhance fisheries and combat malnutrition in one of the world's poorest and most malnourished countries. 

Autonomous Reef Monitoring Structures (ARMS) are small structures consisting of stacked PVC plates that mimic reef habitat to passively attract a diversity of reef species. Originally devised to census reef biodiversity, we used ARMS to collect and transfer the biodiversity necessary to “seed” new reefs. Our team created an accessible ARMS design, transitioning materials from PVC and stainless steel to limestone. We deployed nearly 200 ARMS in the Bay of Ranobe, our research site, engaging approximately 600 community members in the restoration process. We are building six 1-ha artificial reefs and seeding half with ARMS colonized on the healthiest reef in the Bay. This ecosystem-scale experiment is allowing us to comprehensively test the efficacy of ARMS seeding by tracking biodiversity from microorganisms to large predators, quantifying fish catch and effort, and using a prospective cohort study to evaluate human well-being.

We found that microbes and algae were highly correlated on the seafloor, indicating that overfishing is harming reef communities. Reef depth predicted hard coral cover, demonstrating that local fishing pressures are particularly acute on shallow reefs. Nearly 200 fish species were caught in the Bay and the average catch was less than 10 cm long. The small size of harvested fish was not solely because all large fish had already been caught, as is common. Larger fish were caught less often because the most common gear types target smaller fish, gear types which also produce the largest amount of catch per unit effort. Aquaculture is frequently heralded as an alternative livelihood to fishing. In this region, aquaculture is instead an additional livelihood, and not a full time occupation. 91% of people in the region live in poverty compared to the national average of 77%, while childhood stunting was three times higher in inland farming villages relative to coastal fishing villages, highlighting micro-variation in nutrition and the broader challenges of food security in the region. 

Intellectual Merit

The use of ARMS to census reef biodiversity is increasing. We developed an alternative to destructive sampling that leaves ARMS undisturbed by carrying out a standardized visual census underwater, generating multiple benefits from this tool.

Our team designed innovative mixed-methods approaches to assess the intersection of climate and environmental change, coral reef and fisheries conditions, fisher catch and seafood market dynamics, and human dietary intake, nutritional status, and mental health. The model for this research can be used elsewhere to explore the food system and human health implications of environmental change. 

This study represents a unique example of integration across the social-ecological spectrum. That is, we demonstrate the importance of working with communities to characterize not only the dimensions of environmental factors that shape the sustainability of reef ecosystems but also the social factors that determine how community members interact with this environment. 

Our team developed culturally adapted mental health assessment tools for Madagascar in the Malagasy language and we tested them for assessing depression and anxiety symptoms, providing the first validated tools for these issues in Madagascar. This is the first study to empirically evaluate the association between environmental and climate stressors and mental health in fishing communities. 

Broader Impacts

Through education, we have trained over 100 Malagasy undergraduate and graduate students, integrating local knowledge and participation into our research. Approximately 75 undergraduate and MS students took our reef ecology course (lecture and field) and our data science bootcamps. A large number of early-career Malagasy scientists gained hands-on research and scientific training, including one PhD student and five MS students in reef ecology, two PhD students, five MS students, and five technicians in fisheries ecology, and two PhD students and six technicians in human health. The team included 13 others early career scientists, ranging from MS students to postdocs, and originating from seven nationalities. Consortium members were 52% women and 81% are from low and middle-income countries. 

The ARMS and the artificial reefs were translated into design principles for locally adapted reef restoration technologies by local Malagasy scientists. These technologies are being implemented for the first time via this project. ARMS seeding has potential applications in more than 100 countries with coral reefs. If the technology and community engagement can scale, this work can serve as a model for reef habitat restoration as a core intervention in protecting human livelihoods, nutrition, and mental health.

abstractText:
Fish provide the primary source of protein for a billion people, but that crucial food supply is threatened by overfishing. Despite a vast scientific and policy literature arguing that sustainable fisheries are achievable through scientific models and management frameworks, the health of global fisheries continues to decline. This suggests that there may be something fundamentally wrong with the way we have tried to analyze, understand, and manage fishing. This project examines an overlooked but critical factor in the overfishing crisis: the false belief that fisheries are inexhaustible, meaning they can be harvested at contemporary rates indefinitely, year after year, without risk of collapse. The resulting dissertation will: 1) document the history of inexhaustibility and show how resistance to the idea of dwindling fish stocks has taken different forms over the centuries; 2) examine what propels belief in inexhaustible seas; and 3) suggest how its influence might be mitigated to allow for the development of more effective and resilient fisheries management strategies. 

This project finds surprising continuities over a hundred and fifty years of history. Preliminary results from archival research methods show that inexhaustibility appears in diverse forms over time but for similar reasons, including 1) overconfidence in quantitative science and free markets to simplify and solve complex environmental and social problems; 2) failure to account for observed fluctuations in fish populations that may make predictable and sustainable annual catches very difficult in the long term; and 3) an inertia generated by existing models, areas of focus, and management strategies that precludes new ways of thinking. Drawing on historian Thomas Hughes’ notion of technological momentum, this project suggests that the idea of inexhaustibility has had sufficient intellectual momentum that it has proved nearly impossible to dislodge, even in the face of volumes of refuting empirical evidence. Through publications, op-eds, forums, round-table discussions, and oral histories deposited in the NOAA Voices archive, this project will engage scientists, policy-makers, environmentalists, and workers in the fishing industry in rethinking fisheries science to adapt to the reality of an exhaustible—and increasingly exhausted—sea.

projectOutComesReport:
INTELLECTUAL MERITS

This project used archival sources and oral history to interrogate how fisheries science developed historically and why fisheries have been frequently described as “in a state of crisis” despite the guidance of fisheries science. The PIs found that fisheries science co-evolved alongside the industrial fishing industry as a set of tools intended to create and support sustainable industrial fishing. In other words, scientists set out to find the quantities of resources that could be extracted to maximize food production and financial profit. This goal – and the underlying assumption that large sustainable yields were possible – led to a systematic bias towards overly optimistic expectations of large sustainable catches, or a presumption of plenitude. Manifestations of this bias range from scientific assessments and models designed to yield cornucopian visions of fish abundance and disregard ecological complexity, to an “anti-precautionary principle” where the burden of proof falls on those who would propose catch limits. This presumption of plenitude has meant that fisheries have been considered abundant until proven otherwise.

These presumptions are challenged by an inconvenient truth: marine ecosystems are highly complex, and characterized by nonlinear climatic and ecological dynamics. However, the PIs found this data was largely not incorporated into fisheries science and management. Instead, the possibility of sustainable industrial fishing was assumed theoretically rather than proven empirically, and indeed has never been proven empirically. Moreover, the theory underpinning it relied on assumptions which were known at the time to be false, namely a static balance of nature, consistent annual reproduction within fish stocks, negligible population fluctuations in natural populations, and the ability of ecosystem interactions to withstand the removal of 50-75% of the biomass of key species (as fisheries science recommended for maximum productivity). While sometimes helpful in managing heavily fished populations, the enclosure of territorial waters and the implementation and enforcement of quotas did not fundamentally change the presumption of plenitude, as domestic fleets expanded and quotas frequently overestimated both stock size and reproduction rate.

The PIs also found that industry consultants have played and continue to play a large role in both fisheries science and management, including sitting on the scientific committees of regional fishery management organizations and conducting stock assessments. While usually professing dedication to conduct “good science”, consultants also represent the interests of their clients, and the PIs found evidence that consultant-produced stock assessments, catch quota proposals and ecological theories favored the interests of their clients, former clients, potential clients, or general “allies.”

BROADER IMPACTS

The successes and failures of fishery management matter because fish provide the primary source of protein for nearly a billion people worldwide, and many scientists (particularly ecologists) believe the state of marine fisheries is dire. Understanding the history of fisheries science illuminates its limits, and enhances our capacity to make fishing systems more robust and responsive to major fluctuations and sources of uncertainty. Understanding the origins of the presumption of plenitude and the reasons behind its persistence allow us to develop more precautionary, resilient and equitable fishing practices.

abstractText:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this I-Corps project is the development of entry-level, open-ended, soft robotics kits with accompanying curricular materials. The goal of the proposed technology is to enable students and researchers to test and prototype soft robots with an easy-to-use platform. The proposed open-ended kit will include portable and compact control hardware alongside materials and instructions for building soft sensors and actuators.  This information will enable high-school students, undergraduate design teams, and academic and industrial researchers to create their own soft robots, which will enable both education and research applications of soft robotics by students, researchers, and hobbyist-makers.  The proposed technology may be a gateway that can further motivate students to learn about soft robots, engineering, science, and mathematics.  

This I-Corps project is based on the development of entry-level soft robotic kits aimed at middle and high school students that will include materials, building guides, and curriculums to create soft finger-like grippers using tendon and pneumatic actuation methods.  The proposed technology platform includes a catalog of design and fabrication rules for soft robots, guidelines for simulating fluid-structure interaction with finite element modeling, demonstration and validation via hardware, documentation of research results, engineering student education, and an open-source platform for sharing the research with the broader educational and research communities. The kits consist of 3D computer aided design (CAD) models, simulation files, and fabrication instructions that may be adapted for other applications.  Combining soft robotic technology with applications involving human interaction and the use of social and people-centric applications is expected to attract a more diverse population to the study of STEM (science, technology, mathematics, and engineering) subjects.

projectOutComesReport:
The Soft Robotics Toolkit (SRT) is an online resource for soft roboticists and educators, historically providing access to key designs and mechanisms commonly used by this field of research. One of the offerings is the Pneumatic Controller (PC), a controller for simple soft robotic systems, helping researchers and students explore the world of pneumatic soft robots. Another specific kit, the Gripper Kit (GK), was designed for 4-12th grade students. In this experience, students fabricate their own soft grippers from silicone, learning about mold making, casting, robotic actuation, and control. These kits have been tested in classrooms and summer camps and have been developed across several iterations to conform to the needs of teachers and students alike.

Through the National I-Corps program we launched a customer discovery research phase for our kits, interviewing at least one hundred educators, parents, and teachers to better understand the need for novel STEM kits. We identified that interdisciplinary and future-focused kits could inspire students to rethink robotics and were popular with end users and potential buyers. After this program, we focused on expanding the GK as it had many, if not all, of the parameters identified throughout our interview process. Some of the highlights from this project include a collaboration with EXPLO summer camps, giving around 45 kids a hands-on experience with the revised GK. This experience ended with surveys and further redesign of the GK to fit the needs of users. We also redesigned the GK using low-cost materials for ease of manufacturing and to lower barriers to entry for future potential customers. We engaged with MassRobotics and the Boston Museum of Science in multiple outreach events, igniting enthusiasm for soft robotics (and gathering valuable insight into the needs of teachers and their students, as well as parents). We successfully executed an online SRT Design Competition in 2023 and participated in multiple conferences for robotics and education in the Boston area.

Intellectual Merit: The SRT project continues to contribute to the advancement of knowledge in the field of soft robotics. The development of the PC and educational kits like the GK encourage students to explore creative solutions in designing soft robots. Through experimentation and problem-solving, individuals gain practical skills and develop their capacity for innovation. Through the SRT project, we have facilitated collaborations with multiple institutions and summer camps. This collaborative approach enhances knowledge-sharing and the exchange of ideas within the local robotics community. Researchers, students, and educators from diverse backgrounds can come together to learn, experiment, discuss and generate new insights.

Broader Impacts: Our tools and kits serve as educational resources, both for our team as developers learning how to make better educational products, and for the end-users of students and teachers. These experiences actively educate and inspire the next generation of roboticists and engineers through hands-on learning and intuitive design. We reached thousands of students, teachers and parents during the outreach events in 2023, and many reported high levels of engagement and satisfaction with the experience. These events led to additional interviews with interested parties. The SRT kits continue to inspire young learners, particularly in K-12 settings, to engage with robotics and engineering concepts in a unique way. By empowering researchers and students with our SRT kits, the future of the robotics field will have a community of creative thinkers, more commercially viable products and a next generation of innovators with an understanding of the possibilities for robotics.

abstractText:
The goal of this project is to obtain a photosynthetic bioproduction platform that can efficiently convert sunlight and CO2 into bioproducts of interest, through iterative removal of selected genes from a cyanobacterium.  Cyanobacteria are oxygenic photosynthetic prokaryotes that are uniquely poised to become optimal platforms for sustainable bioproduction using sunlight and atmospheric CO2 as well as free and ubiquitous substrates. The genes selected for removal would be identified with the aid of computational methods and gene editing techniques. Gene removal is accomplished without compromising the growth rate of the organism. This project trains several national and international undergraduate students under different collaborative programs, in the design and implementation of molecular tools, relevant computational techniques and physiology of photosynthetic organisms. In addition, the project is designed to align with a variety of scientific entrepreneurial ventures. 

This project develops Synechococcus 2973, a cyanobacterium displaying the fastest photoautotrophic growth ever observed, into an ideal chassis strain by streamlining its genome in a multi-step process that involves state-of-the-art genome-editing technology, guided by experimental analysis and metabolic modeling. Efficacy of reduction is assessed by both growth rate and productivity of a plug-in reporter pathway. Minimizing the genome while retaining fast growth eases the metabolic burden on the strain, removes cryptic regulatory processes that challenge predictable engineering, and improves understanding and control over this powerful autotrophic workhorse. The creation of a novel streamlined model cyanobacterium is a significant step in achieving an industrial “green E. coli” and establishing the foundation for a sustainable bioeconomy.

This award is co-funded by the Systems and Synthetic Biology Cluster in the Division of Molecular and Cellular Biosciences and the Cellular and Biochemical Engineering Program in the Division of Chemical, Bioengineering, Environmental and Transport Systems.

projectOutComesReport:
Cyanobacteria are promising platforms for the sustainable photosynthetic production of natural products and high-value chemicals. However, their adoption as synthetic biology chassis organisms is limited by slower growth rate, limited understanding of their metabolism, and a paucity of genetic tools, relative to heterotrophic model strains. This collaborative project asked whether building a “streamlined” genome cyanobacteria, with a substantial fraction of non-essential elements of the genome removed could improve productivity and potentially simplify cryptic regulation in the cyanobacterial genome, and set out to design, construct, and test streamlined designs. The project succeeded at these core goals, producing cyanobacterial strains with up to 2% of their genome deleted, growing more rapidly (by 23%), and producing more sucrose (by 22%) when engineered to do so than the fastest-growing model cyanobacterial strain described previously. The collaboration of three labs with differing expertise was critical in achieving this aim and in exploring adjacent questions, with expertise across computational modeling, cyanobacterial engineering, and genetic tool development and sequencing technology being strengths of the three labs.

            Unexpected findings during this project spawned new project directions. Modeling predicted contiguous regions of the genome to delete, but difficulty was encountered when deleting long segments of the genome using existing methods. The team instead adapted a distinct technology, Cas3587, to facilitate large genome deletions. This was one of few published examples of this technology, and the first use of this technology in cyanobacteria. This technique generated the strains described in “Genome streamlining to improve performance of a fast-growing cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus UTEX 2973”, but additionally led the Pakrasi Lab to pursue an additional unplanned effort, cyanobacteria antenna reduction using this technology. Antenna reduction in cyano has led to mixed results in the past, but provided benefit in this case, using this new technique. This led to an additional avenue for producing improved phenotype strains, and this study led to ~22% improvement in sucrose productivity, through a distinct mechanism.

            The Church Lab leveraged the cyanobacteria expertise from the Pakrasi Lab and Maranas lab and through collaboration and discussion, this proposal led to independent directions. This award supported in part the Church Lab’s characterization of novel cyanobacteria isolated from marine CO2-emitting volcanic seeps, UTEX 3222. One such cyanobacterium displays unique and industrially-relevant characteristics, including higher density growth than previously reported in other relevant strains and an aggregation/sinking behavior, which appears relevant for biomass harvesting. We anticipate that the genome streamlining methods explored in this work may be relevant across many cyanobacteria. In an additional research direction, the Church lab also integrated cyanobacteria into their experience in hardware and automation, beginning new research directions exploring the automated culture systems that could more easily evolve and characterize improved cyanobacterial strains.

The goal of creating streamlined-genome cyanobacterial chassis strains using the input of three labs not only succeeded at creating improved, genome-streamlined strains. In addition, this proposal generated novel genome engineering techniques for cyanobacteria, helped resolve older debates like antenna reduction, and spawned entirely new efforts in cyanobacterial genome modeling, new cyanobacteria chassis bioprospecting, and development of automated labware for cyanobacteria culture. Taken together, these results push photosynthetic Synthetic Biology biology and applications forward and extend what is possible in this area.

abstractText:
Most research on forests occurs within a single forest or only over a few years or, less often, a few decades. It is typically believed that local disturbances affect trees only in that forest. However, recent evidence suggests that disturbances affected forests over hundreds of miles and more by the same series of drought events and a hard spring frost that occurred 250 years ago. These extreme weather events made it possible for many ancient trees within this region to grow from small saplings into the canopy trees they are now. These large-scale but very short-lived events like drought and frost are predicted to occur more often and become worse in the future. If that happens, regional forest declines could become more important in the future. To see if this is a real possibility, this award will yield new data from old forests throughout the Northeastern U.S. to investigate how trees and forests respond to extreme events similar to those from 250 years ago. The broader impacts will focus on recruiting people who are not well represented in scientific and academic institutions. Students and project participants will be trained on how to conduct science with humility, have respect for all people, and to combat institutional racism and gender bias. The team will be active on social media and make presentations at scientific meetings, public lectures, and educational events to share what is learned through our study.

The ecological memory of forested ecosystems to extreme climatic events is not adequately captured by theories of disturbance and vegetation models; the common scale of ecological research is spatially too small and temporally too short to capture long-term ecosystem development. This award will investigate multiple data streams with two dynamic vegetation models and Bayes hierarchical modelling to answer several questions, including: 1) How do extreme climatic events impact ecosystem development and ecological processes? and 2) What are the long-term interactions between local, high-frequency disturbance (windstorms, gap dynamics, etc.) and large-scale, low-frequency disturbance (severe drought)? Through these questions, the research will rigorously test theory by confronting models with realistic disturbance scenarios from 600 years of tree-growth data covering 400,000 km2 of the northeastern US to determine to what extent extreme climatic events synchronize disturbance across spatial scales and their potential long-term legacies. The award outcomes will be useful in forecasting climate-forest interactions, as extreme events are expected to increase in the future. By scaling from seasons to centuries, this project bridges short- and long-term studies to provide information at the scales necessary to guide land use decisions in complex systems under a changing climate. In addition to training, the project will conduct a modelling workshop to push the margins of forest science by inviting experts and people from a range of disciplines and underrepresented groups to produce a conceptual paper at the intersection of data-model assimilation, Bayesian statistics, and spatial and temporal analyses.

abstractText:
Metabolism supplies the energy and material that living cells use to grow, move, and establish their internal structure. Metabolic fluxes, the rate of turnover of molecules through metabolic pathways, are known to exhibit spatial and temporal variations between cells and within cells, but such heterogeneities remain poorly understood. In this project, the PI will obtain training and perform research that will enable him to transition so that a significant effort in his laboratory is dedicated to studying the spatiotemporal behaviors of metabolic fluxes in cell biology. The knowledge gained may help lead to an understanding of how metabolic defects disrupt cell division, growth, and subcellular organization. The Broader Impacts of the work include the intrinsic merit of the research as all cells undergo metabolic flux and disruptions can lead to diverse pathologies.  In addition, graduate students, undergraduates, and high school students will be trained in interdisciplinary research, both through working on the project, and in classes, summer courses, and tutorials. High school students, and members of the general public, will be given the opportunity to use research grade microscopes to examine the growth and behaviors of algae, and to learn about the connection between single cell organisms and the environment.

This project will enable the PI to shift the focus of his research to a new area at the interface between chemistry, physics, and biology: the nature, causes, and consequences of spatiotemporal variations in metabolic fluxes. In the professional development portion of the project, the PI, and members of his lab, will learn two techniques for measuring metabolic fluxes: mass spectroscopy and stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy. In the research portion of the project, they will use these techniques, along with fluorescence microscopy and coarse-grained theories, to study: 1) the impact of gene expression on temporal and cell-to-cell variation of metabolic fluxes in E. coli, and 2) subcellular variations in mitochondrial metabolism and metabolic fluxes in mouse oocytes. The long-term goal of this work is to develop transformative methods and predictive theories that will provide insights into biological self-organization and the rules governing life's processes.  This work is supported by both the Cellular Dynamics and Function Cluster, along with the Systems and Synthetic Biology Cluster in the Division of Molecular and Cellular Biosciences.

projectOutComesReport:
Metabolic fluxes are known to exhibit spatial and temporal variations between cells and within cells, but such heterogeneities remain poorly understood. Over the course of this project, the PI and members of his lab undertook efforts to study the spatiotemporal behaviors of metabolic fluxes in cell biology. This work involved training in modern biochemical techniques, and the integration of such techniques with approaches from cell biology and physics. These efforts well position the PI and his lab to help develop transformative methods and predictive theories that combine molecular information on metabolism with the complex spatial organization from cell biology and coarse-grained physical theories. The ultimate goal is to gain insight into the nature, causes, and consequences of spatiotemporal variations in metabolic fluxes. The knowledge gained may help lead to an understanding of how metabolic defects disrupt cell division, growth, and subcellular organization, which cause diverse pathologies, including cancer, neurological diseases, and infertility. Over the course of this project, graduate students, undergraduates, and high school students were trained in interdisciplinary research, both through working on the project, and in classes, summer courses, and tutorials. Obtained results were disseminated in research journals and at conferences. Outreach efforts were also undertaken in collaboration with BioBus, a nonprofit, dedicated to engagng the public with hands-on, inquiry-based science.

abstractText:
Northern latitudes are warming at twice the global mean, making carbon stored in permafrost increasingly vulnerable to thaw and decomposition by microbes, potentially leading to large increases in methane (CH4) and carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions, both important greenhouse gases. Accurate and reliable forecasts of greenhouse gas emissions are critical for the improvement of global models that predict changes to temperature and to sea level. On a local level, the data and modeling products can be used to better inform local populations of the changes happening to their environment and help predict likely changes in the future. Improvements to regional and global scale models require advancement in the current knowledge of methane and carbon dioxide flux sources to gain insight into how the net flux is expected to respond to a warming Arctic. Comparing aircraft derived fluxes to local tower measurements and land classification maps allows for the determination of which mechanisms are primarily responsible for the variation in emissions. Data, models, and analysis directly measuring the fluxes over regional scales close to the surface and measuring fluxes using inverse modeling helps to better understand the differences. Data generated from this project are important for evaluating which combination of environmental quantities and categorical quantities are best suited for predicting methane and carbon dioxide emissions to produce more accurate estimates from remotely sensed variables and will also be compared with existing carbon emissions models. The ability to define the current late summer and autumn net flux of methane and carbon dioxide from the North Slope and adjoining Arctic waters is required to establish a benchmark for quantitatively tracking the annual time series of net carbon flux from the Arctic.

This research provides emission measurements of CO2 and CH4 plus nitrous oxide (N2O), and water vapor (H2O) from the North Slope of Alaska on a small aircraft operating at altitudes from 10 m to 10 km, with custom-built spectroscopic sensors, an air turbulence probe, and GPS systems. This project bridges the scale gap between local studies of carbon emissions in the Arctic, such as those from flux towers, and large regional scale emissions estimates from inversion modeling. The work provides resolved emissions correlated with underlying sources; regional coverage for comprehensive analysis of carbon emissions in this part of the Arctic basin; direct coupling of the observations with other observing systems ranging from small tower measurements to satellite remote sensing; and coupling of the observations to an air transport model to compare direct emission measurements to top-down estimates of regional emissions based on profile measurements in the atmosphere. Specifically, aircraft eddy covariance measurements and vertical profiles are used to effectively scale process measurements from short eddy covariance towers to the regional scale, allowing for determining how representative certain areas are of the larger North Slope with respect to flux of the major gases that contribute to changes in radiative forcing. Observations and modeling of fluxes and concentrations of molecules that differ in their isotopic composition reveal the contributions of key source processes at local, landscape, and regional scale, a feature unique to this project. This project creates an analysis framework to allow for the combination of in situ concentrations and fluxes with regional fluxes calculated using a transport model that both is adapted for Alaska and widely applicable to other circumpolar areas.

orgLongName: Directorate for Geosciences
projectOutComesReport:
The Arctic is warming at twice the global mean, making organic matter frozen in the permafrost increasingly vulnerable to thaw and decomposition by microbes, which in turn produce methane or carbon dioxide as a byproduct. The carbon, in the form of organic matter, stored in the Arctic region represents nearly twice the amount of carbon currently in the atmosphere. Understanding this potential for carbon release depends heavily on understanding the biological and physical processes that control the lability of the frozen carbon and the production and oxidation of the carbon as it’s converted to carbon dioxide or methane and how these processes may vary across the Arctic.

This project sought to measure the amount of, or flux, of these gases coming from or into the northern soils from several different regions of the Alaskan North Slope. In order to do this, we outfitting a van with with custom built instruments that used absorption spectroscopy to measure the amount of gases in the ambient air, specifically carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, and water vapor. In addition to the main instruments we installed a small tower on top of the van with a sonic anemometer, a device that measures the three dimensional wind speed, as well as ambient air temperature. Using this along with pressure and a GPS system for absolute position and heading we are able to calculate the flux of gases using a technique called eddy covariance. Using high resolution winds from the anemometer we can add up the upwelling and downwelling wind, along with the associated gas concentration, to get the net amount of that gas that is coming up from the ground or going into the ground.

In addition to the in situ measurements, we also employed models to study emissions integrating in situ and remote sensing data both for the current data set as well as past measurements. Traditional methods that assume homogeneous landscapes can bias carbon flux estimates in Arctic tundra, overestimating CO₂ uptake and underestimating CH₄ emissions. By using Bayesian MCMC methods, footprint models, and high-resolution land-cover maps, this study shows that accounting for landscape heterogeneity improves flux estimates and regional carbon budget accuracy. The Alaska North Slope is neither a consistent carbon sink nor source, with CO₂ fluxes varying between -6 and +6 Tg C per year (2012–2017), largely influenced by biogenic emissions from unfrozen soils and inland waters during the early cold season. This study highlights the importance of year-round CO₂ flux monitoring across diverse Arctic ecosystems to improve projections of carbon dynamics under future warming.
